Auf diesem Kanal reisen wir zurück in die Vergangenheit und erinnern uns an die kleinen Dinge, die früher zum Alltag gehörten – an alte Haushaltsgegenstände, vergessene Gerichte, besondere Kindheitserinnerungen, verschwundene Läden, frühere Gewohnheiten und Geschichten, die heute fast niemand mehr erzählt.
Hier geht es um die 60er, 70er, 80er und 90er Jahre, um das Leben von damals, um Omas kluge Haushaltstricks, Opas praktische Tipps und um all die Momente, die viele Menschen noch tief im Herzen tragen.

channels.title: Gloria's Kitchen Table
channels.description:
I'm Gloria. I'm seventy-five years old, and everything I know about a stove I learned standing at
my mother's elbow.

She fed nine people on eight dollars a week and never wrote down a single line of it. She thought
there'd be time. She died on a Tuesday and I stood in her kitchen afterwards and couldn't find
one recipe in her handwriting.

So this table is where I say it out loud before it goes. Every day I sit down and go back into
those kitchens — the suppers, the Sunday dishes, the foil pans that went to church, the fish fry
on a Friday — and I name the food our mothers and grandmothers made, and what it felt like to eat
it.

I'm not a chef. I have no license and no restaurant. I'm a woman who was there.

The recipes are written out complete in my cookbook, in large print:
honestvoicesbooks.com

New memories every day.

Somebody fed you. Say her name.

Old Australia covers the economic and social decisions that transformed one of the world's most prosperous nations into a country where ordinary Australians can no longer afford to live the way their parents did

We cover housing affordability, the cost of living crisis, manufacturing decline, energy privatisation, superannuation, the age pension, Australian wages, and the stories behind the headlines that rarely get told in full.

If you remember when a single income bought a home, when power bills were an afterthought, when retirement was something you could actually plan for, this channel is for you.

New documentary every week.

channels.title: Fin del Mapa
channels.description:
Fin del Mapa es un canal documental en español sobre lugares extremos, islas remotas, territorios abandonados, naufragios, pueblos olvidados y expediciones que terminaron lejos de todo.

Contamos historias reales marcadas por el aislamiento, la supervivencia, la geografía y el abandono: personas olvidadas en islas perdidas, comunidades que desaparecieron, desastres silenciados, colonias fallidas y rincones del mundo donde la naturaleza y el tiempo borraron casi todas las huellas.

Cada documental busca responder una pregunta: ¿qué ocurre cuando un lugar queda tan lejos, tan aislado o tan olvidado que el mundo deja de mirar?

Fin del Mapa es un viaje por los límites de la civilización, la memoria y la resistencia humana.

channels.title: Ayer Vivo
channels.description:
En este canal contamos la historia de España a través de quienes la vivieron de verdad: familias, barrios y pueblos que sostuvieron el país con trabajo diario, mucho antes de que nadie hablara de desarrollismo o de progreso.

Cada video reconstruye una época concreta — la posguerra, los años del desarrollismo, la Transición — a partir de la economía doméstica real: lo que se ganaba, lo que costaba, lo que una familia podía permitirse con un solo sueldo y lo que esa vida exigía a cambio.

No buscamos nostalgia fácil. Investigamos cada dato, cada precio en pesetas, cada oficio y cada costumbre antes de contarlo, y tratamos esas vidas con el mismo respeto con el que nos gustaría que alguien contara la nuestra.

Historias para quienes quieren entender de dónde viene la España de hoy, y para quienes todavía recuerdan de dónde vino.

channels.title: Am Werkstor
channels.description:
Willkommen bei Am Werkstor.

Hier geht es um die Unternehmen, die die elektronische Welt gebaut haben – und darum, was aus ihnen geworden ist.

In jeder Folge erzählen wir die Geschichte einer einzigen Firma: wie sie entstand, wer sie aufbaute, welches Produkt alles veränderte und an welchem Punkt die Sache kippte. Dokumentarisch und ohne Eile, meist 30 Minuten.

Uns interessieren nicht nur Vorstände und Quartalszahlen, sondern vor allem die Menschen hinter den Geräten: die Ingenieure, deren Namen in keiner offiziellen Firmenchronik stehen, obwohl sie das Entscheidende gebaut haben.

Wir arbeiten mit Daten, Zahlen und nachprüfbaren Quellen. Und wenn sich eine Entscheidung auf zwei Arten lesen lässt, zeigen wir beide.

Themen: Computer und Heimcomputer, Prozessoren und Halbleiter, Telefone und Mobilfunk, gescheiterte Giganten und stille Weltmarktführer.

Für alle, die diese Geräte noch selbst benutzt haben – und für alle, die wissen wollen, warum es sie heute nicht mehr gibt.

Sixty years on one pit in Marshall, Texas. Fire, wood, meat, beans, and the things nobody tells you.

I'm James J. Conner. I cook on the old Highway Eighty, east of town, on a pit I welded myself in 1988. My grandmother put me on the fire when I was nine. She never taught me a recipe. She taught me wood.

Nineteen years on second shift at the tire plant, selling plates out the front yard on weekends. Forty-one pits built for other people. The shop burned in 2003 and I cooked out of a trailer nine years.

Every week, how this actually works. Brisket and ribs, and what goes beside them: beans, greens, cornbread, the pot and the fire under it. I'll tell you when I'm certain and when I'm guessing, and which tricks I don't use myself.

East Texas. Chopped beef, sauce on it, hickory and sweet gum. Sauce is not an apology.

Use a thermometer. I go by hand. You shouldn't.

channels.title: Otis's Kitchen
channels.description:
My mother ran a farm kitchen outside Cedar Rapids and fed eight people a day out of it. She never owned a recipe card. Everything she knew was in her head, and when she died in 2004 most of it went into the ground with her.

I'm Otis. I spent forty years picking barns and estate auctions across the Midwest, so I know what it looks like when something valuable gets thrown out because nobody recognized it. This channel is me getting down what I can of hers before it goes the same way.

The tricks, not the recipes. Why cold hands make layers. Why the skillet has to be screaming. What a farm wife did with half a pound of sausage and eleven men at the table.

Some of it the food scientists have caught up to and explained. Some of it was just a woman with one hog, one cow and eleven miles of gravel between her and a store. And where she had the right rule for the wrong reason, I'll say so — I'd rather be useful than romantic.

New video every week.

channels.title: Mrs. Doris
channels.description:
I'm Mrs. Doris. For thirty-five years I stood behind a school lunch line in southern Ohio and fed four hundred kids a day on a dollar and five cents a tray. The shoe factory closed, the steel mill closed, and my lunch count went up - my budget never did. So I learned every trick there is: the poor man meals, the Depression-era recipes, the meat stretchers, the one-pot suppers our grandparents used to survive.

 If you are cooking for one, two or a whole crowd on a tight budget - grab a tray. You are in the right line.

Four hundred kids a day and not one of them went hungry. Neither will you....

channels.title: Burl Sizemore
channels.description:
Hi, I'm Burl Sizemore.

I was born in 1954 and have spent my whole life in the same county in the mountains of eastern Kentucky. My father came home from the Pacific in 1946 to a house with no electricity, no running water and a mule in the lot. I watched all three go in a decade.

This channel is about what a man carried in his pockets and what he did with it. The knives, the stones, the small tools, and the fixes that came before you could buy another one.

I am not here to tell you the old ways were wisdom. They were what was available. When something better showed up, these were not stubborn people. But every so often they threw out a thing that was better, and nobody checked. Those are worth a look.

Everyday carry, pocket knives, hand tools, sharpening, Appalachian household objects, forgotten repairs, and life in these mountains from the 1930s to the 1960s.

New videos regularly.

Subscribe if you carry something in your pocket that your grandfather would recognize.
